BIS Quarterly Review, September 2026

Yields climb, yet risk appetite holds firm

In the review period flare-ups in geopolitical tensions tested the positive momentum that had characterised the first half of the year. Markets faced bouts of volatility as hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz heightened uncertainty about the inflation and monetary policy outlook. On top of that, lingering concerns about the sustainability of fiscal burdens added to the pressure. The prospects of higher rates stemming from these macroeconomic challenges compounded markets’ unease about valuations and possible overinvestment in the tech sector, disrupting the equity momentum driven by artificial intelligence (AI). Yet while investors’ risk appetite ebbed and flowed, it proved resilient on the whole.

Frank Smets and Gaston Gelos summarise the September 2026 BIS Quarterly Review and answer journalists’ questions about market developments, the state of the global economy and fiscal policy.

Puriya Abbassi explains how private credit helped finance the post-2020 shift to the digital economy.

BIS Quarterly Review, March 2026

Markets recalibrate amid shifting currents

During the review period, financial markets had to adjust to shifting currents. Even though markets initially appeared calm on the surface, there were significant shifts under the surface as investors rotated away from previously high-performing assets. Volatility began to creep up, exacerbated by the conflict in the Middle East in early March.

Global equity markets saw regional and sectoral shifts in late 2025, with investors moving away from US large cap and growth stocks. European and Japanese equities posted gains, while emerging market economy (EME) equities saw an even greater boost. Despite solid earnings, concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending and disruption weighed on richly valued technology companies. Value and small cap stocks outperformed. While index volatility rose, it was eclipsed by significantly greater individual stock volatility.

Hyun Song Shin summarises the March 2026 BIS Quarterly Review and, along with Gaston Gelos and Frank Smets, answers journalists' questions about market developments, the state of the global economy and fiscal policy. Read more here .

Matthieu Chavaz provides an overview of the challenges central banks face and the tools they can use to maintain clarity, credibility and accountability in the face of uncertainty.

titulo: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
contexto_listado: BIS Working Paper No 1383 16 Oct 2026 Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets… By Gerardo Ferrara , Andreas Schrimpf , Ganesh Viswanath-Natraj and Zijie Wang
texto:
Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets

Focus

We study how trading in offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets for emerging market currencies transmits to onshore spot exchange rates. We also assess how capital controls and the ability of domestic banks to trade offshore affect that transmission. Our analysis uses transaction-level data on NDF trades cleared through LCH ForexClear for 10 emerging market currencies from 2014 to 2025.

Contribution

This paper is the first to analyse NDF price formation using signed, transaction-level order flow rather than quoted rates or aggregate trading volumes. We develop a model in which two forces operate separately: offshore demand to gain currency exposure, which moves prices and the gap between offshore and onshore rates together, and the cost faced by banks that intermediate between offshore and onshore markets, which moves that gap relative to prices. Four episodes in which regulators changed banks’ access to offshore NDF markets – in China, Malaysia and, twice, in India – illustrate both channels at work.

Findings

A $1 billion increase in offshore dollar demand moves the onshore exchange rate by about 10 basis points within minutes, and the offshore forward rate by about 18 basis points. Offshore trading also widens the gap between offshore and onshore prices, in line with our model’s predictions. This gap narrowed, for instance, when Indian banks were allowed to participate in offshore markets in 2020 and widened again when that access was restricted in 2026. The results show that offshore trading affects onshore exchange rates even where capital controls limit direct access to the domestic market, and that how much of this pressure reaches the domestic market depends on how tightly banks’ cross-market activity is regulated.

Abstract

We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread. To our knowledge, this is the first transaction-level evidence on price formation in these markets. A $1 billion long-USD order flow depreciates the domestic spot rate by about 10 basis points and the offshore NDF rate by about 18 basis points. The spot impact is larger when dealer balance sheets are tight. Policy episodes in the Chinese renminbi, Malaysian ringgit, and Indian rupee show how changes in offshore speculative activity and arbitrage between offshore and onshore markets affect the spread and domestic exchange rates. We rationalize these findings with a model in which offshore demand pressure generates NDF order flow, dealers hedge inventory through domestic spot markets, and capital controls limit intermediation between offshore and onshore forward markets.

Authors



Head of Financial Markets

Monetary and Economic Department, Financial Markets

titulo: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
contexto_listado: BIS Working Paper No 1382 13 Oct 2026 Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes? We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market… By Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro Innovation and fintech
texto:
Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?

Focus

Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value, usually against the US dollar. Like bank deposits, they can provide payment and liquidity services, but they generally pay little or no interest. We examine whether stablecoins and bank deposits compete for users’ funds by studying how stablecoin demand responds when banks change the rates they offer on deposits.

Contribution

Using weekly US data from January 2019 to June 2025, we relate changes in bank deposit rates to subsequent changes in the market capitalisation of reserve-backed stablecoins. Our analysis controls for broader interest rate conditions, Treasury yields, exchange rate movements, bitcoin prices, financial market volatility and developments in cryptocurrency markets. It also exploits the non-linear way in which banks pass changes in policy rates through to deposit rates in order to address possible two-way causality.

Findings

Our results provide evidence that stablecoins and bank deposits are partial substitutes. Higher deposit rates are followed by slower stablecoin growth, with the relationship being stronger for USDC than for USDT. The results remain when considering different deposit products and stablecoins supplied to decentralised finance protocols, and are not found for non-stablecoin cryptoassets. These findings suggest that bank deposit pricing may influence the growth of the stablecoin sector and that, if stablecoins become more widely used, they could affect banks’ funding conditions and the transmission of monetary policy. The analysis concerns the allocation of funds between assets and does not establish that stablecoin growth necessarily reduces aggregate bank deposits or lending.

Abstract

We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through. Whereas other money market rates track the federal funds rate roughly linearly, banksreprice deposits more aggressively once it exceeds approximately 3%. Against average ten-week stablecoin growth of 15%, ordinary least squares estimates imply a reduction of roughly 3 percentage points per basis point of deposit repricing, or about 3.75 percentage points per one-standard-deviation move. Instrumental variable estimates are roughly three times larger and pass a placebo test using non-stablecoin cryptocurrencies. Effects are stronger for USDC than for USDT, consistent with the former’s closer ties to U.S. depositors. Cross-sectional variation in repricing across deposit tiers provides independent evidence of substitution. The size of the stablecoin sector therefore depends in part on howbanks price deposits.

Authors



Principal Economist

Monetary and Economic Department, Financial Stability Policy

contexto_listado: BIS Working Paper No 1381 12 Oct 2026 Transformative AI and demand bottlenecks Transformative AI promises to accelerate growth through productivity enhancement and automation. Yet automation on such a scale… By Phurichai Rungcharoenkitkul Innovation and fintech
texto:
Transformative AI and demand bottlenecks

Focus

Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to substantially boost economic growth. When transformative, AI could automate an expanding set of tasks, improve machines’ capability and unlock the endogenous growth engine. Some recent estimates suggest growth could exceed 10% within a few years under such transformative scenarios. At the same time, large-scale automation could absorb resources, diverting more output to investment at the expense of consumption. Could AI sustain higher growth even as households buy a smaller share of total output?

Contribution

We examine demand bottlenecks as a possible constraint to otherwise transformative AI. We employ a task-based endogenous growth model where innovation is driven by rents on consumer products. As automation advances, the consumption share and the associated rents decline, weakening incentives to innovate further with AI. The framework allows for several scenarios depending on how fast AI technologies arrive and how long rents last, among other factors. Evidence on these parameters provides discipline in assessing the scenarios. The model also has implications for the natural rate of interest and the broader AI debate.

Findings

We identify several AI scenarios. Under “transformative AI”, growth takes off, reaching 5.5% after two decades and continuing to rise. Under “demand bottleneck”, growth accelerates briefly before falling below the pre-AI rate of 2% as innovation permanently slows. Other scenarios similarly point to, at best, moderate gains in growth, far below the transformative AI outcome. The calibrated model points to the demand bottleneck scenario as empirically highly plausible. The range of possible outcomes underscores the high uncertainty about the natural rate of interest.

Abstract

Transformative AI promises to accelerate growth through productivity enhancement and automation. Yet automation on such a scale would raise the share of investment in output, potentially starving AI innovation of returns from a shrinking consumer market. We propose an endogenous growth framework to study this interaction, featuring research and entry decisions that propel AI advances but whose costs must be paid for by consumer demand. We identify several scenarios, spanning transformative AI, a demand bottleneck outcome where thinning consumer demand stalls AI progress, and intermediate cases in between. When anchored to evidence, the calibrated model points to the demand bottleneck as a highly plausible scenario, and projects more moderate growth in the coming years relative to recent studies such as Korinek et al. (2026). We draw policy implications, including for the natural rate of interest.

Authors

Principal Economist

Monetary and Economic Department, Macroeconomic Analysis Unit
